rv.q: Tamsin Greig is shatteringly good in Terence Rattigan’s 1952 tragedy of quiet desperation.
It’s a delicate, sensitive revival of Rattigan’s compassionate masterpiece.
She can turn on a sixpence between mad laughter and crumpled hysteria.
This revival, much praised at the tiny Ustinov theatre in Bath, has virtues aplenty but it hasn’t scaled up fully now it is in the grander Theatre Royal Haymarket.
The result is a perfectly decent production of a pretty much perfect play.
But for its emotional agonies to really torture us, I was hoping for a more intimate atmosphere than is provided by Lindsay Posner's respectable production, first seen in Bath last year.
Telling the story of a destructive affair, Terence Rattigan’s stinging 1952 drama is a sensitively observed classic, underserved by this stiff, overly mannered production.
It’s a terrific production that reveals the extraordinary power in this slightly old-fashioned play that has outlasted many more modish works.
The play itself endures as a matchless portrait in soldiering on in sadness, until such time, presumably, as you simply can't.
Tamsin Greig, as always, seems to be performing a role that was written with her in mind.

Posner directs Rattigan’s play with sensitive precision, from the striking first image of Hester lying prone in front of the gas fire, a shaft of light under the front door illuminating the gloomy room, to the loaded silences, which reveal as much as the characters’ tense exchanges.
The story drags on ever so slightly, but a talented cast and clever direction make it a compelling, thought-provoking watch.
In Greig’s performance, either outcome would be validated by the hours before, and that is her triumph.
This production is a devastatingly intimate portrait of love, despair, and the quiet agony of emotional isolation.
It's a solid revival of one of the most touching plays from the era, but at times it feels like a historical re-enactment.

cn.t: Greig delivers a powerful, nuanced performance in this generally well-regarded revival of Rattigan's classic, though some critics find Posner's production overly mannered and struggling to fill the larger West End space.
